title: Reform Movements of the 19th Century

cards.b: Before political nationalism there was a social awakening. UPSC loves matching reformers, organisations, books and years, and asking about their method and limits.

Reformist movements used reason and law to fight sati, child marriage and caste. Revivalist ones went back to the past (the Arya Samaj’s “Back to the Vedas”). Both worked in the shadow of colonial rule, missionaries and English education. Hindu, Muslim, Parsi, Sikh and Christian reformers all took part.

cards.h: Raja Ram Mohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj
cards.b: Founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Samaj (1828). Opposed sati, idolatry and polytheism. Lord Bentinck outlawed sati in 1829 (Regulation XVII). Roy wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin and published Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar. Debendranath Tagore revived the Samaj (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839). Keshub Chandra Sen split it in 1866. The Native Marriage Act 1872 followed.

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: Widow Remarriage Act 1856; girls’ schools.
  • Derozio and Young Bengal: free thought.
  • Ramakrishna and Vivekananda: Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Vivekananda spoke at Chicago in 1893.
  • Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang; Ranade, Bhandarkar).
  • Gopal Hari Deshmukh “Lokahitawadi” and Jotirao Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873).

Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (Bombay, 1875), with Satyarth Prakash as its book. His slogan: “go back to the Vedas”. He opposed idol worship, caste by birth and child marriage, and ran the shuddhi movement. Lala Hansraj started the DAV schools (1886 at Lahore).

Theosophical Society: Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott (New York 1875; Adyar 1882); Annie Besant led it and founded the Central Hindu College (1898) and the Home Rule League.

• Aligarh: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College (1875).
  • Deoband: Muhammad Qasim Nanotvi (1866) — religious purity, later aligned with Congress.
  • Ahmadiyya (1889), Mirza Ghulam Ahmad; Wahabi, Syed Ahmad Barelvi.
  • Parsi: Rahnumae Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851), Naoroji and Behramji Malabari.
  • Sikh: Singh Sabha (1873); Akali movement, 1920s.

Reformers used journals, schools, petitions and legislation. Achievements: sati ban 1829, widow remarriage 1856, Age of Consent Act 1891 (raised to 12 after Malabari’s campaign), Special Marriage Act 1872, Sarda Act 1929. Limits: mostly urban and upper caste; ignored the lowest castes and peasants; rarely questioned colonial rule. Some reformers’ religious revivalism fed communal identities.

Historians such as Sumit Sarkar question the word “renaissance”. Others see in these movements a rational base for nationalism, as Bipan Chandra argues. Dalit and feminist scholars say the reformers’ concerns were partial: they looked at women through upper-caste reform, and Phule and Ambedkar had to push further.

The reform legacy underlies the Constitution’s Articles 14 to 17 and 25 to 28, the Hindu Code Bills (1955 to 56), and the Supreme Court’s 2018 Sabarimala and 2017 triple talaq (Shayara Bano) judgments. Debates on a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) echo reformers’ questions.

• “The 19th century reform movements were both reformist and revivalist. Discuss.”
  • “Role of Raja Ram Mohan Roy in modernising India.”
  • Prelims tip: match organisation to founder and year; Brahmo 1828, Prarthana 1867, Arya Samaj 1875, Satyashodhak 1873, Theosophical 1875.
